episodes.203139: A new multi-day plume of monsoon moisture advected northward into New Mexico between an upper level trough over the southern Baja Peninsula and an upper high over the south-central CONUS. Daily rounds of afternoon thunderstorms producing heavy rain developing over the mountains of New Mexico before moving over surrounding lower elevations through the evening resulted in several events of flash flooding and isolated reports of large hail. Rainfall rates of 4 inches per hour totaling 2 inches in 30 minutes produced flash flooding in Magdalena on July 20th. The Cochiti Golf Course experienced flash flooding July 21st. The highest coverage of thunderstorms during this period occurred July 22nd with thunderstorms moving over the Ruidoso area burn scars just after sunset. Flash flooding and debris flows on and below the South Fork and Salt burn scars resulted in brief road closures. The Albuquerque metro experienced flash flooding from heavy rainfall rates of 2 inches per hour totaling 1 to 1.50 inches in 30 minutes over the North Valley neighborhood. Finally, thunderstorms producing heavy rainfall on July 24th directly over the South Fork burn scar totaling just over 2 inches produced flash flooding and debris flows down Cedar Creek and the Rio Ruidoso to Ruidoso Downs.
episodes.203260: A push of monsoon moisture into southeast Wyoming lead to the development of widespread showers and storms that eventually converged over the city of Cheyenne. Intense rainfall lead to impressive rainfall rates, resulting in urban flooding across the city.
episodes.203327: Heavy precipitation on July 23rd resulted in a steep increase in the river level of the South Branch Tributary of Mud Creek near Rauville.
episodes.203496: A surge of monsoon moisture brought strong thunderstorms to southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska the afternoon and evening of July 24th. Strong winds, hail, and flash flooding were reported with storms.
episodes.203499: A surge of monsoon moisture brought strong thunderstorms to southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska the afternoon and evening of July 24th. Strong winds, hail, and flash flooding were reported with storms.
episodes.203517: A line of thunderstorms produced strong winds over the bay of Green Bay and Lake Michigan during the evening hours on Wednesday (7/23).
episodes.203830: Scattered thunderstorms produced significant wind damage across portions of the Chicago Metro area during the afternoon of July 24th.
episodes.203831: Scattered thunderstorms produced localized severe winds across portions of northwest Indiana during the afternoon of July 24th.
episodes.203832: Scattered severe thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the afternoon of July 24th.
episodes.204076: Severe Thunderstorms moved across Weld, Morgan, and Adams County. Most reports were from the Greeley area where hail reached 1.25 inches and minor flooding was reported.
episodes.204606: Scattered thunderstorms developed across the South Plains and Rolling Plains regions late in the afternoon on the 24th underneath a mid-level monsoon moisture plume. Very little atmospheric wind shear contributed to the short lived nature of this thunderstorm activity. A couple of storms produced severe wind gusts in Parmer and Cottle Counties as they collapsed to the surface.
episodes.204784: The setup today was similar to that of July 21st and 22nd. Scattered thunderstorms developed in a weakly forced environment and moved off the higher terrain to the northeast across Southeast New Mexico and the Permian Basin. Dry low-levels allowed for a severe wind gust in the Davis Mountains.
episodes.205457: On the afternoon of July 23rd, 2025, scattered thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska, spurred by a cold front pushing into the western part of the state and an approaching shortwave disturbance. As the afternoon transitioned into the evening, these thunderstorms merged into a mesoscale convective complex (MCS) that moved into east-central Nebraska. This complex found a favorable environment with abundant instability, moist mid-levels, and steep low-level lapse rates, which promoted an area of severe wind gusts, particularly in Boone and Platte counties. Radar imagery from this period also showed a descending rear inflow jet, a feature often associated with strong winds in these types of storms. The impacts of the storm included a measured 61 mph wind gust reported two miles west of St. Edward at 7:40 PM CST, followed by a fire department report of uprooted trees and downed power lines in St. Edward at 7:45 PM CST. The complex continued its eastward path, and a public report from Wisner at 8:42 PM CST noted broken tree limbs measuring six to eight inches in diameter. The storm then moved into western Iowa, with no further reports of damage.
episodes.205619: Evening sea breeze convection within southeast flow well to the east-southeast of an area of disturbed weather centered near the Mississippi Delta along the north-central gulf coast produce gusty winds over Tampa Bay area waters.
episodes.205641: Deep moisture interacted with diurnal temperatures in the mid to upper 90s to produce an isolated severe storm.
episodes.205650: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms associated with an inverted trough moved across the region. A couple strong wind gusts along the coast occurred.
episodes.205723: Discrete thunderstorms from northeast Illinois and northwest Indiana congealed into a line of storms as it tracked east-northeast. Thunderstorm wind gusts and the outflow wind ahead of the line resulted in instances of downed trees.
episodes.205990: Dying thunderstorms produced heat burst wind gusts during the late evening and early morning hours. Later afternoon convection produced damaging wind gusts that were detected by SD mesonet stations.
episodes.206000: A weak upper level trough moved through southern New Mexico combining with an already moist atmosphere.  Slow moving storms developed over the Sacramento Mountains and brought heavy rain to the Mescalero Indian Reservation which caused  flash flooding southeast of Mescalero.
episodes.206046: During the late afternoon and early evening of July 23rd, thunderstorms formed over the northeastern Texas Panhandle into the far eastern Oklahoma Panhandle. As these storms moved east to northeast the atmosphere supported strong thunderstorms that could produced severe wind gusts. Some of these thunderstorms produced wind damage that could have resulted from winds up to 80mph.
episodes.206079: Several clusters of storms moved from central South Dakota into Minnesota during the morning, then more widespread coverage of storms developed and persisted throughout much of the day. The main axis of heavy rainfall was tied to a slow moving boundary that started across central Minnesota in the morning and progressed towards southern Minnesota by the late evening.||While many locations saw heavy rainfall amounts and rainfall rates at times, two main spots reported flash flooding impacts. This included the city of Albany in Stearns County and the Skyline area just south of Mankato in Blue Earth County. ||There was also an isolated funnel cloud report with a storm that moved through Waseca County that did not produce a tornado.
episodes.206176: A cluster of thunderstorms erupted within a very moist and unstable airmass ahead of a slow moving frontal boundary during the evening of July 23. These thunderstorms bisected the city of Sioux Falls from southwest to northeast with neighborhoods southeast of I-229 reporting 2 to 5 inches of rain in a matter of 1-2 hours. This resulted in significant flash flooding across impacted portions of the city. Later in the evening, a large mesoscale convective system across Nebraska moved north and east, bringing heavy rain to portions of southeast South Dakota. Additional localized flash flooding was observed after midnight in Beresford, South Dakota.
episodes.206408: Dewpoints in the upper 60s and lower 70s, combined with temperatures |in the low to mid 90s, resulted in widespread heat index values of 100+ degrees which fueled scattered severe thunderstorm development late in the day.
episodes.206411: Thunderstorms moving through Saginaw Bay produced wind gusts in excess of 50 knots.
episodes.207027: On the evening of July 23rd, 2025, a weak wave passed along a southwest to northeast oriented boundary draped over western and northwestern Iowa, increasing convergence and initiating storms within a highly unstable environment. Slow storm motion, resulting from a relatively weak kinematic environment, combined with abundant mid- and upper-level moisture to produce efficient rainfall. Rainfall amounts of 4 to 6 inches were measured in northern Iowa. Minor flooding in low-lying areas occurred, but no significant flash flooding was reported.|This environment, characterized by meager effective shear and heavy rainfall, led to rapid cold pool production and outflows outpacing storms. While this limited the threat of widespread wind damage, sporadic downburst winds occurred with thunderstorms firing along the outflow, resulting in isolated tree damage in the town of Corwith early in the evening. Wind damage was also reported later in the evening as storms moved through Ankeny and Bondurant, damaging trees, shingles, and displacing loose objects in town.|In addition to these downburst winds, an interaction between thunderstorm outflow dropping southward from northern Iowa, and the cold pool with the main wave tracking eastward out of western Iowa produced a small but persistent enhancement of surface winds along their intersection. This resulted in a narrow swath of damaging winds starting near Willey in Carroll County, then tracking east-southeastward through Coon Rapids and south of Bayard and Bagley. Wind gusts of 65 to 75 mph were measured along this swath, resulting in mostly tree damage, as well as damage to one hog confinement near Willey.
episodes.207946: Warm, and very moist air mass in the Midwest, combined with a front slowly leaning into the region, resulted in development of upstream convection that, even after decaying earlier in the day, was enough of an atmospheric perturbation to kick off another line of thunderstorms. This line crossed Lake Michigan during the late evening hours on the 23rd. This line resulted in gusty winds and thunderstorm wind damage, particularly across northwest Lower Michigan.
episodes.207947: A highly unstable atmosphere over the Midwest, combined with a subtle boundary draping into the Upper Midwest on the morning of the 24th, resulted in development of a thunderstorm complex that crossed northern Lake Michigan and tracked through the Tip of the Mitt region. A mesovortex embedded within the complex tightened in the vicinity of Pellston, resulting in several reports of a possible funnel cloud in the vicinity of Weadock and Riggsville in rural, northern Cheboygan County though no tornado damage was discovered during the storm survey.
episodes.207948: Later in the afternoon on the 24th, a line of storms, associated with the morning storms across the Tip of the Mitt, developed across the southern/southeastern portions of the forecast area, resulting in pockets of tree damage from northeastern Gladwin county and Ogemaw county, eastward to Lake Huron.
episodes.207953: A line of thunderstorms that produced wind damage across parts of Gladwin, Iosco, and Arenac counties, continued eastward over Lake Huron late in the afternoon.
episodes.207957: Warm, and very moist air mass in the Midwest, combined with a front slowly leaning into the region, resulted in development of upstream convection that, even after decaying earlier in the day, was enough of an atmospheric perturbation to kick off another line of thunderstorms. This line crossed Lake Michigan during the late evening hours on the 23rd. This line resulted in gusty winds and thunderstorm wind damage, particularly across northwest Lower Michigan.
